rejected.title: First Nations knowledge in managing landscapes
card: Traditional Owners are the First Nations people whose Country a place is. Their knowledge of fire, plants and animals has been built up and passed on over many generations.
Kakadu and Uluru-Kata Tjuta national parks are jointly managed. Traditional Owners and Parks Australia make decisions together, through boards with a Traditional Owner majority.
Fire knowledge guides burning. Small, cool fires lit at the right time of year leave a patchwork of burnt and unburnt ground, and reduce the fuel for big, hot fires later.
Knowledge of plants and animals guides other care, such as knowing when food plants are ready and where animals breed.
rejected.remember: Joint management puts Traditional Owners' knowledge to work in caring for the land.

a.q: Who makes decisions about caring for Kakadu National Park?
opts: Traditional Owners and Parks Australia together
Parks Australia alone, after hearing advice
Traditional Owners alone, with no agency role
The tour companies that bring in visitors
a.why: Kakadu is jointly managed, so Traditional Owners and Parks Australia make decisions together. Parks Australia deciding alone after advice is tempting, but joint management means the decisions are shared.

b.q: Rangers at Uluru-Kata Tjuta want to protect a rare plant from big, hot fires. Which approach best fits the park's joint management?
opts: Plan small, cool burns with Traditional Owners
Stop all burning so fire never reaches the plant
Burn the whole area at once in the hottest month
Let Parks Australia plan burns alone, then report
b.why: Small, cool burns reduce the fuel for big, hot fires, and planning them with Traditional Owners uses their fire knowledge, as joint management intends. Stopping all burning lets fuel build up, which makes a big, hot fire more likely.
b.clue: Think about fuel, and about who shares the decisions.

version.title: First Nations knowledge in managing landscapes
card: Traditional Owners are the First Nations people whose Country a place is. Their knowledge of fire, plants and animals has been passed down over many generations.
Kakadu and Uluru-Kata Tjuta national parks are jointly managed: Traditional Owners and Parks Australia make decisions together, through a board with a Traditional Owner majority.
Fire knowledge guides burning. Small, cool fires lit at the right time of year leave a patchwork of burnt and unburnt ground, which cuts the fuel for big, hot fires later.
Knowledge of plants and animals guides other care, such as knowing where animals live and breed, and tracking them to check how they are going.
version.remember: Joint management uses Traditional Owners' knowledge to guide how the land is cared for.

a.q: Why do rangers in Kakadu light small, cool fires at the right time of year?
opts: To cut fuel for big, hot fires later
To burn every plant so none grow back
To stop any fire starting there again
To clear space for roads and buildings
a.why: Small, cool fires leave a patchwork of burnt and unburnt ground, which cuts the fuel for big, hot fires later. They do not burn every plant, because they leave unburnt patches.
a.clue: Think about what a big fire needs to burn.

b.q: Rangers in Kakadu notice fewer of a small native animal in one area. Under joint management, which plan fits best?
opts: Decide with Traditional Owners, using their knowledge
Let Parks Australia decide alone, then inform others
Ask Traditional Owners only after the plan is set
Leave the area alone, as people should not manage it
b.why: Joint management means Traditional Owners and Parks Australia make decisions together, and Traditional Owners' knowledge of animals guides care. Asking them only after the plan is set is tempting, but then the decision is not shared.
b.clue: Who makes decisions in a jointly managed park?

a.best: To cut fuel for big, hot fires later

b.best: Decide with Traditional Owners, using their knowledge
